q: What is the most common cause of Cushing syndrome in older patients?
o: A benign pituitary macroadenoma causing hormone deficiency
explanation:
The most common cause of Cushing syndrome in older patients is iatrogenic supraphysiologic corticosteroid dosing (p1526, p1530).

D. Autoimmune adrenalitis: This causes primary adrenal insufficiency, not the most common Cushing syndrome (p1531).
A. Rapid withdrawal of chronic glucocorticoids: This is the most common adrenal-insufficiency mechanism in older patients (p1526, p1531).
B. A benign pituitary macroadenoma causing hormone deficiency: A large benign macroadenoma is a common cause of chronic hypopituitarism (p1529).

q: What is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency in older patients?
o: Rapid discontinuation of chronic glucocorticoid therapy
explanation:
Rapid discontinuation of chronic glucocorticoid treatment is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency in older patients (p1526, p1531).

A. Autoimmune adrenalitis: Although a common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in industrialized countries, it rarely occurs in older patients (p1531).
B. Tuberculosis affecting the adrenal glands: This remains common worldwide but is very rare in older residents of industrialized countries (p1531).
C. Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage: This can occur in older anticoagulated patients, but iatrogenic suppression and withdrawal are the most common cause (p1531).

q: At what size does a pituitary incidentaloma become a "macroincidentaloma" requiring a fuller hormone-deficiency workup?
o: At any size, with no cutoff
explanation:
A pituitary macroincidentaloma of at least 1 cm warrants careful evaluation for pituitary hormone deficiency (p1529).

A. Only above 4 cm: Greater than 4 cm is an adrenal-incidentaloma malignancy concern, not the pituitary macroincidentaloma threshold (p1532, p1529).
B. Only below 1 cm: The book uses at least 1 cm for a large pituitary macroincidentaloma (p1529).
C. At any size, with no cutoff: The fuller hormone-deficiency evaluation is specified for a large lesion of at least 1 cm (p1529).

q: What CT finding on an adrenal incidentaloma excludes malignancy and pheochromocytoma?
o: Any radiodensity in an incidentally discovered mass
An adrenal mass larger than 4 cm
explanation:
Low adrenal-incidentaloma radiodensity from fat content, below 10 Hounsfield units on CT, excludes malignancy and pheochromocytoma in the book (p1532).

D. Higher radiodensity requiring biochemical evaluation: Higher-density incidentalomas must be assessed for pheochromocytoma (p1532).
B. An adrenal mass larger than 4 cm: Masses larger than 4 cm are more likely to be malignant (p1532).
A. Any radiodensity in an incidentally discovered mass: All incidentalomas require assessment; the exclusion described is low radiodensity below 10 units (p1532).

q: At what hematocrit should testosterone therapy be reduced or stopped?
explanation:
A hematocrit greater than 54% during testosterone treatment warrants dose reduction or discontinuation (p1535-1536).

B. 10% to 15%: This is the fraction of primary hyperparathyroidism due to diffuse hyperplasia, not a hematocrit cutoff (p1536).
C. 80%: This is the single-adenoma fraction in primary hyperparathyroidism, not the testosterone cutoff (p1536).
D. Less than 5%: This describes the fraction due to multiple parathyroid adenomas, not a hematocrit threshold (p1536).

q: Is PSA/DRE monitoring recommended for a 74-year-old man starting testosterone therapy?
o: Yes - all men aged 70 or older require routine PSA/DRE screening
No - such screening is not recommended at age 70 or older
No - testosterone treatment rules out screening at every age
Yes - short life expectancy strengthens the routine screening indication
explanation:
PSA/DRE monitoring for prostate cancer is not recommended in testosterone-treated men aged 70 or older, or with life expectancy below 10 years (p1536).

A. Yes - all men aged 70 or older require routine PSA/DRE screening: The book specifically advises against this screening in testosterone-treated men 70 or older (p1536).
C. No - testosterone treatment rules out screening at every age: In men younger than 70, PSA monitoring is a shared decision (p1536).
D. Yes - short life expectancy strengthens the routine screening indication: Life expectancy below 10 years is another reason screening is not recommended (p1536).

q: What proportion of primary hyperparathyroidism cases are due to a single parathyroid adenoma?
explanation:
A single parathyroid adenoma accounts for 80% of primary hyperparathyroidism cases (p1536).

C. 10% to 15%: This is the proportion due to diffuse parathyroid hyperplasia (p1536).
A. Less than 5%: This is the proportion due to multiple parathyroid adenomas (p1536).
D. Less than 1%: This is the proportion due to parathyroid carcinoma (p1536).

q: What serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level defines vitamin D sufficiency per the American Geriatrics Society (used for fall/fracture prevention in frail older adults)?
explanation:
The AGS definition used for fall and fracture prevention in frail high-risk older adults is serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D greater than 30 ng/mL (p1539).

B. Greater than 20 ng/mL: This is the Institute of Medicine sufficiency definition for general-population bone health (p1539).
C. 12 to 20 ng/mL: The Institute of Medicine defines this as insufficiency (p1539).
A. Less than 12 ng/mL: The Institute of Medicine defines this as deficiency (p1539).
